summary:
This record covers Sud, a region of Italy, and stands under the national framework of the Italian Republic. Outright International records same-sex relations as legal throughout Italy for men and women, a baseline that has not prevented recurring violence against LGBT people and in particular against transgender people. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Annual Review documents that homophobic and transphobic violence continued in 2025, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes in which groups lure victims and then assault or rob them. Progetto Gionata characterises transphobia as the most severe and most widespread discrimination confronting transgender people in Italy.

ILGA-Europe's annual country review for Italy, published in February 2025, finds a troubling increase in both the number and the geographic spread of bias-motivated violence against LGBTI people during 2024, with incidents reported almost monthly rather than confined to isolated episodes. Violence of this kind is recorded within Sud itself. The same review reports a scooter-mounted assault on a young man in Scampia, a district of Naples, in March 2025. On 13 October 2025 Il Gazzettino reported that a 63-year-old man was arrested in Torre Annunziata, in the province of Naples, after making stabbing threats against a young LGBTQIA+ activist, an incident the newspaper characterised as a grave homophobic episode in the Naples area.

The most serious traveller-specific finding is the sexual assault of young transgender tourists in Campania, within this region. ANSA reports that the convictions for the assault were upheld on appeal in April 2026, an outcome that affirms accountability for violence against trans visitors while also confirming that the assault took place and that the victims were targeted while in Italy. The dating-app entrapment schemes that ILGA-Europe records nationally present a comparable risk surface for transgender visitors who use dating and hookup applications, where victims are deliberately isolated before being attacked.

Transgender people in Italy face a documented risk of physical violence from the officers who stop them. On 5 July 2024 tgcom24 reported that a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to ten months in prison for stopping and then beating a transgender woman with batons, a conviction showing that such conduct reaches criminal sanction.

Detention carries no dedicated trans provision. Italy has no specialised prison for transgender inmates: the plan announced in 2010 to convert an almost empty medium-security prison at Pozzale near Florence was never realised, and trans detainees remain within the ordinary men's and women's prison circuit. The Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report of July 2025 sets out the legal and policy framework governing LGBTIQ detainees in Italy, the pathways available for gender affirmation in custody, and the treatment of same-sex relationships in prison, while a 2026 study in Frontiers in Psychiatry, drawing on a thematic analysis of transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons, records systemic gaps and institutional challenges in the care provided to incarcerated trans people.

The political and institutional climate is openly hostile. ILGA-Europe reports that Italy's Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from its Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second consecutive year, and that a cardinal described homosexual acts as a mortal sin. Human Rights Watch's 2025 World Report chapter on Italy records sustained hostile political rhetoric about LGBT people as contributing to a hostile environment, within a wider account of rule-of-law and civil-society constraints in the country.
tangentialFactors:
Two judicial and law-enforcement developments outside Sud indicate the direction of the national framework. In March 2025 the Civil Court of Asti recognised, for the first time in that court, the physical and psychological harm caused by homophobic mistreatment; the recognition concerns the setting the case arose from and its reach beyond that court is not established by the source. The ten-month prison sentence imposed on a Milan traffic officer for beating a transgender woman with batons, reported on 5 July 2024, likewise concerns another region but bears on how trans people are treated by police nationwide.

The violence pattern recorded in Sud matches the national monitoring picture rather than departing from it: ILGA-Europe reports incidents almost monthly across Italy during 2024, with a rising geographic spread, while the documented incidents in this region (Scampia, Torre Annunziata, Campania) cluster around Naples and its province. Organised entrapment schemes targeting gay men, recorded nationally in 2025, indicate an organised dimension to the risk rather than opportunistic incidents alone.
localsOnly:
Transgender residents held in custody are placed in ordinary men's or women's facilities. In January 2010 the BBC reported that Italy would open one of the world's first prisons dedicated to transgender inmates at Pozzale, near Florence in Tuscany, converting an almost empty medium-security prison to house trans inmates, mainly those convicted of drug-related offences and prostitution, a plan gay-rights groups welcomed at the time. Reporting in 2013 indicates the prison had not been created, and this Pozzale initiative remains the only documented Italian special-unit proposal for trans prisoners, announced but never opened.

Progetto Gionata's assessment that transphobia is the most pervasive discrimination facing transgender people in Italy is a resident-facing finding, describing a condition of daily life rather than a visitor-specific hazard. The Ludwig Boltzmann Institute report of July 2025 and the 2026 Frontiers in Psychiatry study address the care and legal position of LGBTIQ detainees as residents of the prison system, documenting systemic gaps in gender-affirming provision and in psychiatric care.
outOfScopeNotes:
The date sequence in the ILGA-Europe material is unresolved: the annual country review for Italy carries a February 2025 publication date yet is cited for an assault that took place in March 2025. The sources do not reconcile this, and the underlying report should be checked before either date is relied on.

The status of the Pozzale facility is documented only up to 2013. No later source in this inventory confirms whether any unit for trans prisoners opened after that date, so the current position rests on the absence of any subsequent reporting rather than on a recent official statement. The Pozzale claim itself appears in a Wikipedia section on LGBTQ people in prison and is corroborated only by BBC reporting from January 2010.

The composition of Sud as a jurisdiction is not stated by these sources; every regional incident recorded here falls in Campania, around Naples and its province, so no findings are sourced for the other areas the label may cover. The reach of the Civil Court of Asti's March 2025 recognition beyond that court is not established by the source, and no source in this inventory reports on the practical outcome of the April 2026 appeal beyond the convictions being upheld.
